nodes.label: Azure — East US
nodes.notes: Attacker VM sits on a huge egress pipe (often 10-40 Gbps) with low local latency. Almost none of that capacity can actually be applied to this target.

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.notes: Generates requests / attack traffic. Its OWN bandwidth is effectively irrelevant — the achievable rate is set downstream, on the target side.

nodes.label: Public internet
nodes.notes: ~75-90 ms round-trip US <-> UK. Latency caps per-connection throughput via the bandwidth-delay product: even on fat links, a single TCP flow is limited by window size / RTT. More RTT = less speed per connection.

nodes.label: UniFi Gateway
nodes.notes: CEILING 1 — the 1 GbE WAN uplink: ~940 Mbps usable TCP, hard maximum. CEILING 2 — NAT / port-forward + connection tracking (and IPS/DPI if enabled) add per-packet CPU cost and a finite session-table size. New-connection rate and pps are capped here, not just bandwidth.

nodes.label: Web server VM
nodes.notes: CEILING 3 — 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM. Must actually build every response: TLS, app logic and worker/thread limits cap requests/sec well before the link fills.

nodes.label: Hypervisor + NVMe VHDX
nodes.notes: CEILING 4 — the VHDX lives on NVMe. Storage IOPS / latency and the virtual switch add a further ceiling under load (random I/O, logging, cache misses).

nodes.label: Effective speed = min(all target hops)
nodes.notes: The attacker's real throughput is the SLOWEST link in the chain on the target side: 1 GbE WAN, then firewall NAT/IPS + session limits, then the VM's CPU/RAM, then NVMe I/O. Azure could push far more — the target dictates the rate.

steps.note: Scenario: an attacker running from a VM in Azure East US (USA) targets a web service in the UK. The intuition 'the attacker is on a fast cloud pipe, so it's fast' is wrong — let's follow where the speed is actually decided.
The attacker side looks unlimited: an Azure VM can have 10-40 Gbps of egress. But raw egress is only usable if everything downstream can accept it — it can't. This number is a red herring.

First reality check — the internet in between. US<->UK is ~75-90 ms round-trip. Because of the bandwidth-delay product, a single TCP connection's throughput is capped by window size / RTT. High latency alone throttles per-connection speed no matter how fat the pipes are.
Ceiling 1 — the target's 1 GbE WAN. Everything must funnel through the UniFi gateway's single gigabit uplink: ~940 Mbps usable, a hard maximum. The attacker's 10+ Gbps instantly becomes <1 Gbps here.

Ceiling 2 — the firewall itself. Port-forwarding is NAT plus connection tracking (and IPS/DPI if enabled). That adds per-packet CPU cost and a finite session table, so new-connections/sec and packets/sec are limited here too — not just bandwidth.

Ceiling 3 & 4 — the web VM and its storage. HTTP is forwarded to web01 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM), which has to build every response (TLS, app logic, worker limits) — capping requests/sec. Its VHDX sits on NVMe, so storage IOPS/latency and the vSwitch add one more ceiling under load.

Punchline: the attacker's effective speed = the SLOWEST hop on the target side (1 GbE WAN -> firewall NAT/IPS -> VM CPU/RAM -> NVMe I/O), further throttled by transatlantic latency. The attacker doesn't control the rate — the target's weakest link does. To go faster you must remove the target-side bottleneck; to defend, you deliberately keep those ceilings low (rate-limits, connection caps, WAF).
